description: Create beautiful statistical graphics with Seaborn. Master scatterplots, heatmaps, boxplots, and multi-plot grids using concise, high-level code.

slides.title: Statistical Data Visualization
slides.content:
# Why Seaborn? 🌊

Matplotlib is the foundational plotting library in Python, but it requires a lot of code to make plots look good and to calculate statistics.

**Seaborn** is built *on top* of Matplotlib. It provides a high-level, elegant interface designed specifically for statistical data exploration.

It integrates flawlessly with Pandas DataFrames and automatically applies beautiful color palettes and themes.

slides.title: Loading Data
slides.content:
# Built-in Datasets 📊

Seaborn comes with several famous datasets built-in, making it incredibly easy to practice.

```python_not
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load the 'tips' dataset (a Pandas DataFrame)
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")

print(tips.head(3))
# Output:
#    total_bill   tip     sex smoker  day    time  size
# 0       16.99  1.01  Female     No  Sun  Dinner     2
# 1       10.34  1.66    Male     No  Sun  Dinner     3
# 2       21.01  3.50    Male     No  Sun  Dinner     3
```

slides.title: Relational Plots
slides.content:
# `scatterplot` 🔵

Relational plots show the relationship between two numerical variables.

```python_not
# Plot total_bill on the X axis, and tip on the Y axis
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip")

# You MUST call plt.show() to render the plot!
plt.show()
```

Just by passing the DataFrame to `data=` and the column names as strings, Seaborn extracts the data and labels the axes automatically!

slides.title: Adding Dimensions with Hue
slides.content:
# The Magic of `hue` 🎨

In Matplotlib, coloring dots based on a third variable requires a complex loop. In Seaborn, you just pass the column name to the `hue` parameter.

```python_not
# Color the dots differently based on whether they were a smoker
sns.scatterplot(
    data=tips, 
    x="total_bill", 
    y="tip",
    hue="smoker" # Magic!
)
plt.show()
```

Seaborn automatically assigns contrasting colors and creates a Legend for you!

slides.title: Line Plots
slides.content:
# `lineplot` 📈

Line plots are perfect for visualizing trends over time.

If your dataset contains multiple readings for the exact same X value, Seaborn's `lineplot` will automatically calculate the mean and plot a shaded region representing the 95% Confidence Interval (the statistical uncertainty)!

```python_not
flights = sns.load_dataset("flights")

# x is the year, y is the number of passengers
sns.lineplot(data=flights, x="year", y="passengers")
plt.show()
```

slides.title: Categorical Plots
slides.content:
# `boxplot` 📦

Categorical plots show the relationship between a numerical variable and one or more categorical variables.

A **Boxplot** is the standard way to display the distribution of data based on a five-number summary (minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum), and it easily highlights outliers.

```python_not
# Show the distribution of 'total_bill' for each 'day' of the week
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x="day", y="total_bill")
plt.show()
```

slides.title: Violin Plots
slides.content:
# `violinplot` 🎻

A Boxplot only shows summaries. It hides the underlying shape of the distribution.

A **Violin Plot** combines a boxplot with a KDE (Kernel Density Estimate), drawing a smooth curve that shows exactly where the data is most dense.

```python_not
sns.violinplot(data=tips, x="day", y="total_bill")
plt.show()
```

Fatter sections of the violin indicate a higher density of data points at that value.

slides.title: Matrix Plots
slides.content:
# `heatmap` 🌡️

A Heatmap takes a 2D matrix of data (often a correlation matrix) and visualizes the values using a color gradient.

It is an essential tool in Machine Learning for quickly spotting correlations between features.

```python_not
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Create a 10x10 matrix of random numbers
data = np.random.rand(10, 10)

# annot=True prints the exact numbers inside the colored squares!
sns.heatmap(data, annot=True, cmap="coolwarm")
plt.show()
```

slides.title: The Ultimate Overview
slides.content:
# `pairplot` 👯

When exploring a brand new dataset, you want to see the relationship between *every single* numerical column at once.

`pairplot` does exactly this. It creates a massive grid where the diagonal shows the distribution of a single variable, and the off-diagonals show scatterplots between every pair of variables.

```python_not
iris = sns.load_dataset("iris")

# Creates a 4x4 grid of plots instantly!
sns.pairplot(data=iris, hue="species")
plt.show()
```

slides.title: Multi-plot Grids
slides.content:
# `FacetGrid` 🪟

What if you want to create 4 separate scatterplots, one for each 'day' of the week?

You use a **FacetGrid**. It splits your dataset into subsets based on a categorical variable and maps a plotting function onto a grid of subplots.

```python_not
# Create a grid with 1 column per 'day' (Thur, Fri, Sat, Sun)
g = sns.FacetGrid(tips, col="day")

# Map the sns.scatterplot function onto the grid
g.map(sns.scatterplot, "total_bill", "tip")
plt.show()
```

slides.title: Figure Level vs Axes Level
slides.content:
# Understanding the Architecture 🏛️

Seaborn has two types of functions:

1. **Axes-level functions** (`scatterplot`, `boxplot`): They draw onto a single specific Matplotlib Axes. They cannot create multiple subplots themselves.
2. **Figure-level functions** (`relplot`, `catplot`, `displot`): These wrap `FacetGrid` under the hood. They CAN create grids of subplots automatically!

```python_not
# Instead of building a FacetGrid manually, use the figure-level 'relplot'
# It automatically creates a column for each day!
sns.relplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", kind="scatter", col="day")
```

slides.title: Themes and Styling
slides.content:
# Making it Beautiful ✨

Seaborn allows you to change the entire aesthetic of your plots globally with a single function call.

```python_not
# Set the aesthetic style ('darkgrid', 'whitegrid', 'dark', 'white', 'ticks')
sns.set_style("whitegrid")

# Set the color palette
sns.set_palette("husl")

# Set the context (scales fonts/lines for different mediums)
# Contexts: 'paper', 'notebook', 'talk', 'poster'
sns.set_context("talk")

# Now, all subsequent plots will use these settings!
sns.boxplot(data=tips, x="day", y="total_bill")
```

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Seaborn Master! 🎉

You've learned how to turn raw DataFrames into beautiful statistical graphics.

## Key Takeaways

- ✅ **Integration:** Seaborn is built on Matplotlib but accepts Pandas DataFrames directly via the `data=` parameter.
- ✅ **Dimensions:** Use the `hue` parameter to instantly add a third dimension (color) based on a category.
- ✅ **Plot Types:** Use `scatterplot` (relationships), `boxplot`/`violinplot` (distributions), and `heatmap` (matrices).
- ✅ **Pairplot:** The fastest way to explore a new dataset by plotting every numerical variable against every other one.
- ✅ **Figure-level Grids:** Use `relplot` or `catplot` with the `col` parameter to instantly generate multi-subplot `FacetGrid` figures.

Next, we'll learn how to make our plots interactive!
